newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela - preparing to let go.
newsitem.headline: Mandela - preparing to let go.

text.p: In a world short of true heroes, Nelson Mandela's unbowed courage and open-hearted capacity to forgive inspire an admiration that approaches reverence.
But in South Africa, needing more than just a warm glow to solve its daunting problems, he must in the end be accepted as a mortal man, capable of error and not everlasting.
Easing a young and uncertain democracy towards realisation of that fact is a vital step in preparing South Africa for the fast-approaching day of Mandela's retirement in 1999.

Most analysts dismiss the notion that Mandela's eventual departure will open up a dangerous, dizzying void. There is leadership potential in the wings and a top-level succession well prepared, they point out.

But none deny that Mandela, 78, has unique international stature, that he is still idolised by much of the masses, or that an inexperienced cabinet still seems tempted to toss its hottest potatoes into the Old Man's lap.

More than six years after his release from an apartheid prison, and halfway through a five-year mandate, the Mandela magic lives; his charm, noble spirit and Gandhi-like status as father of a "rainbow" nation of all colours.
But euphoria has faded as new challenges supplant old triumphs, and to his own great relief, people have stopped treating Mandela like some infallible deity.

Where any criticism was once virtually taboo, the president is now taken regularly to task for perceived faults, including excessive loyalty to old allies, remoteness from the executive, irascibility, arrogance, bending over backwards to appease a fearful white minority, resting on his laurels and making promises the government cannot keep.
With foresight on the day of his release, Mandela predicted his most difficult task would be persuading the world he was not "a messiah or a demi-god" but simply a man.
Ever since, he has wrestled to convey a sobering, anti-cult message while simultaneously using his gifts to inspire South Africans with courage and optimism.

Results have been mixed. There is concern, mainly abroad, that the country is over-dependent on him, unsure who will unite it when he's gone, who will shepherd the majority through wrenching economic change or beyond delayed expectations.
In a recent cover story on the country's halting progress, Time magazine called Mandela an extraordinary leader who had become "an overadulated icon".
British political commentator William Rees-Mogg made the call back in June that "Mandela's party is over".
He warned that South Africa urgently needed "some administrative grip" and advised foreign investors that "it never does help to fund a flight from reality".
In its recent mid-term assessment, South Africa's Financial Mail also worried about over-dependence, saying the Mandela name was "sometimes invoked as a mantra".
In an interview, the president agreed: "People still expect me to do more than is humanly possible," he told the weekly.
These days, Mandela is frequently slated for his refusal to dismiss Alfred Nzo and Nkosazana Zuma, the foreign and health ministers widely attacked for incompetence or poor judgment.
By some he was seen as cold and autocratic for dumping Bantu Holomisa, a loyal favourite but a firebrand who dared to criticise the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Critics demand to know where are the 2.5 million houses Mandela promised to build for the homeless, what he intends to do to arrest the crime wave, speed up privatisation, boost economic growth and create jobs.

Their message is clear enough: Mandela, however great a man, is no miracle-maker for South Africa's tough, post-honeymoon transition phase. He provided the essential feel-good factor but now is the time for dynamism and decisiveness.
By the prevailing standards of Western politics, the criticism is usually gentle, the tone duly respectful.

On a more cynical note, South African author Rian Malan recently dared to ask whether Mandela's famously positive impact on all he encounters was not "the mark of a politician too cowardly to court disfavour".

Mandela offered no more than "charming gestures (which) do little to address the underlying problems", Malan wrote in Esquire magazine. "But no matter. They hold us together, keep us more or less sedated," he concluded gloomily.
Mandela's defenders might argue that a society with a history of violence that was undergoing such tumultuous change was very much in need of such sedatives.
After a lifetime of fighting for his people's rights, the diehard campaigner emerged from 27 years in prison in 1990 as world champion of freedom.

He was victorious over a despised apartheid regime yet ready to extend a hand to his enemies in the name of reconciliation. The white rightwing backlash and the vengeful black bloodbath of South Africa's worst nightmares were avoided. "It's a great story, Shakespearean in scope, and deeply moving," said Malan. "What a pity for mythmakers that the saga didn't end there."
Luckily for South Africa, Mandela has not only secured an honoured place in history, he also possesses that dignity, rare in high politics, of knowing when to quit.
He is pressing ahead with a very public schedule for phased withdrawal from active politics and a belated homecoming to the tranquil private life he sacrificed for a multi-racial society.

In little over a year, he will give up leadership of the ANC. He will not seek a new term when his five-year mandate expires in 1999. His chosen successor, Thabo Mbeki, is groomed and readied for anointment.

To underscore his determination to bow out, Mandela recently made public his romance with Graca Machel, widow of Mozambique's late president Samora Machel, who now spends two weeks of every month in his company.
It may be a rather conventional happy ending, but it is surely a better beginning to the next millennium than the world dared hope for South Africa when Mandela was kept behind bars.
